newsitem.title: UK: Good start to spring for West European grains.
newsitem.headline: Good start to spring for West European grains.

text.p: Spring weather in many areas means that grain crops in western Europe are looking good, farming analysts said.
Winter damage to crops already in the ground has been minimal, while farmers are getting on with planting spring crops.
Reuters corespondents questioned analysts in several countries for a west European crop update as of early March.
In France's Paris grain belt, mild weather since early February allowed winter crops to make up for ground lost earlier in the season and crop potential looks good, French crop analysts said.
Winter wheat and barley largely escaped damage from a frost in late December-early January. But cold temperatures pushed back development by some three weeks when compared to last year.
"The mild weather has allowed the crop to make up for development delays. There are no major problems at this stage," a government crop analyst in the region said.
"All we hope for is that the warm and sunny weather will continue. Crop potential at this stage looks good to very good."
Mild weather also allowed farmers to start spring sowings, mostly barley, on schedule in early March but analysts said it was premature to provide a sowings estimate for spring barley.
Winter durum wheat suffered heavy damage in the north and south of the central French Beauce region, analysts said.
They said farmers may have to replant a good part of the 27,000 hectares sown to winter durum, though the impact would be muted because durum output is marginal in the Paris basin.
Durum sowings are expected to decline by 6,000 hectares this year mostly because the region exceeded its maximum guaranteed area for 1996.
Latest sowing estimates dated March 7 indicate winter wheat sowings rose three percent to 790,000 hectares in Paris region.
Winter barley sowings are expected to jump 15 percent to 150,000 hectares and winter rapeseed sowings by 15-20 percent to 165,000 hectares.
For France as a whole grain office ONIC has predicted a 4.4 percent rise in winter grain sowings to 6.75 million hectares.

Winter wheat sowings are expected to rise by 4.6 percent to 4.98 million hectares, winter barley sowings by 5.4 percent to 1.12 million hectares and winter durum sowings by 1.5 percent to 273,000 hectares.

UK farming analysts expressed general satisfaction, despite a shortage of moisture. "We could do with a lot more rain," one said. "If it stays dry during March, people will start to get more worried," he said.
But the overall picture was not so bad, he said. One positive result of low rainfall levels was a high soil nitrogen content, which meant crops were green.

Poor conditions during January and February delayed spring barley sowing. "Drilling's been later than we'd have liked, after a shocking start to the year," one said. But now the delay was being made up. "People have been drilling like mad," the analyst said.
German farmers are planning a swift spring planting campaign in March to take advantage of warm and dry conditions, the DWD national meterorological office said.
"Conditions are ideal, soils are dry and the warmth will aid germination," a source in the farm weather section said.
Farmers will start with spring barley, followed by some spring rapeseed and wheat, while sugar beet plantings typically begin at the end of the month. Maize and sunseed plantings start in April.

The DWD source added winter grains and oilseeds were developing slowly but steadily, and winter damage appeared limited. Maximum daytime temperatures over the next seven days will be in a 13-20 degree range.

Spain's wheat crop in the southern region of Andalusia may be substantially lower this year because of damage and sowing delays during floods, a spokesman for a regional farmers' group said on Monday.

"In principle, the evaluation of the 1997 crop in terms of size won't be good because after the floods earlier this year around 20-30 percent (of ground) couldn't be sown, and then there was damage because of the wet weather," a spokesman for ASAJA said.
Andalusia produced around 75 percent of Spain's 1.7 million tonne durum wheat crop in 1996, and about nine percent of the nation's soft wheat, according to Agriculture Ministry figures.
The crop now faces further problems after six weeks of very dry weather which followed the January flooding, he added.
Maize and barley will escape some of these problems as they are planted later, he said.
Wheat should be ready for harvest some time after mid-May.
--Compiled by Christopher Lyddon in London (+44 171 542 7928), with contributions from Paris, Hamburg and Madrid
